title: The Complexity Analyzer
description: How the built-in Complexity Analyzer reads your blocks and reports Time and Space Big-O -- and how to act on what it tells you.

sections.title: Introduction to Scalability
sections.content: A quick thought experiment: your code runs perfectly on a list of 10 items, in a fraction of a second. What happens on a list of 10,000? Or 10,000,000? Producing the *correct* output isn't the whole job -- you also need to know how the amount of work grows as the input grows. That question has a name: scalability, and it's what this lesson is about.

subsections.title: The Complexity Tab
subsections.content: The workspace's Complexity tab automatically reads your blocks and reports two numbers, both in a notation called Big-O: **Time Complexity** (how the number of operations scales) and **Space Complexity** (how memory use scales). You'll build both intuitions in this lesson using the activities from **Task 1**, where a Constant-Time evaluation is your very first hands-on example.

subsections.title: The Complexity Graph
subsections.content: Below the two scores, the Complexity Graph plots the theoretical Big-O curve for your logic -- it's a prediction based on your block structure, not a live trace of an actual run. An O(n²) result draws a steep, upward-curving line, making it immediately visible just how much performance degrades as the input grows.

sections.title: Understanding Time Complexity
sections.content: Time complexity measures how the number of operations grows as input size -- written `n` -- grows. It focuses on the worst case, drops constant factors, and cares only about the overall trend, not the exact number of steps.

subsections.title: Standard Time Complexities
subsections.content: Four classes you'll see constantly, in order from fastest to slowest:
bullets: **O(1) Constant:** the same fixed amount of work regardless of input size -- e.g. a formula, or looking something up by its exact index.
**O(n) Linear:** work scales one-to-one with the input -- e.g. one loop through a dataset, checking every item once.
**O(n²) Quadratic:** work scales with the *square* of the input -- e.g. a loop nested inside another loop, where every outer step re-runs the whole inner loop.
**O(log n) Logarithmic:** the amount of data left to search shrinks at every step -- e.g. Binary Search, which you'll meet properly in Module 3.

subsections.title: Visualizing Quadratic Growth
subsections.content: Picture a group chat where every person messages every other person exactly once: 5 people means 5 x 4 = 20 messages; add a 6th person and it jumps to 30. That's the shape of quadratic growth -- small additions to the input cause disproportionately large jumps in work. Build a nested loop yourself in the workspace (**Task 2's** "Loops Inside Loops" activity) and watch the Complexity Graph draw that exact same compounding curve.

sections.title: Understanding Space Complexity
sections.content: Time isn't the only resource an algorithm spends -- it also needs memory to run. Space complexity measures how much *extra* memory your algorithm needs beyond the input itself, and managing it well is a mark of thoughtful design, not just correct design.

subsections.title: Allocation versus Mutation
subsections.content: Appending to an array as the input grows requests fresh memory for every new item -- that's **O(n) Space**. Updating a variable that already exists, or swapping two values in place, needs no new memory at all -- that's **O(1) Space**. The difference comes down to a simple question: are you creating new storage, or reusing what you already have?

sections.title: System Tools for Optimization
sections.content: Knowing your algorithm's Big-O is only half the story -- knowing what to do about it is the other half. Two tools in the workspace help with exactly that:

subsections.title: The Big O Reference Modal
subsections.content: The **Big O Reference** button in the footer opens a full reference table covering every complexity class the analyzer detects, with definitions, real examples, and their growth-rate graphs side by side.

subsections.title: Resolving Algorithmic Bottlenecks
subsections.content: A bottleneck is the one piece of logic dragging down your algorithm's entire rating -- often just one loop out of several. Summing a sequence of numbers with a loop is O(n); swapping in a closed-form formula (like the classic `n * (n+1) / 2` for consecutive integers) collapses that same task to O(1). Spotting where a formula could replace a loop is one of the most valuable optimization skills you'll build in this course.

sections.title: Lesson Summary
sections.content: The Complexity Analyzer turns the shape of your blocks directly into a scalability verdict, no extra effort required on your part. Optimizing well means watching both Time and Space together, not chasing just one number.

subsections.title: Analytical Workflow
subsections.content: A simple loop to follow whenever you're checking your own work:
bullets: 1. Build your logic on the canvas.
2. Open the Complexity tab to see the Big-O verdict.
3. Check the growth curve on the Complexity Graph.
4. If it's steep (e.g. O(n²)), isolate and refactor the nested logic causing it.
5. Check the Big O Reference table for a faster alternative.
